entities.name: Jan Roháč of Dubá
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Roháč of Dubá, a Bohemian Hussite general and nobleman, emerged as one of the most steadfast and uncompromising leaders of the radical Hussite faction, the Taborites, in the final tumultuous phase of the Hussite Wars (1419–1434). His defiance, particularly after the decisive defeat of the Taborite forces at the Battle of Lipany in 1434, solidified his image as a symbol of unyielding resistance against both Catholic imperial power and the moderate Utraquist Hussites. His life and dramatic end represent the last gasp of the radical Hussite dream for a truly reformed Bohemian society, profoundly influencing the memory of the Hussite movement within Czech national consciousness.

Following the catastrophic defeat at Lipany, where the Taborite army was largely annihilated, Jan Roháč refused to accept the Compacts of Basel, the agreement between moderate Hussites and the Catholic Church, which he viewed as a betrayal of Jan Hus's original tenets. He retreated to his fortified stronghold, Sion Castle, near Kutná Hora, gathering remnants of the radical Hussite forces and continuing a guerrilla campaign. This final act of rebellion provoked a major siege in 1437, led by the forces of the newly crowned King Sigismund of Luxembourg. Despite a valiant defense, Sion Castle fell after a prolonged assault, and Roháč was captured.

His capture and subsequent execution by hanging in Prague on September 18, 1437, marked the definitive end of organized radical Hussite military resistance. While the moderate Utraquist wing of Hussitism continued to exist legally for decades, Roháč's demise closed the chapter on the revolutionary, militant phase of the Hussite Wars, allowing for a period of consolidation and political compromise within Bohemia. His legacy, however, transcended his military defeat, transforming him into a martyr and a potent symbol of national self-determination and religious conviction against overwhelming odds.
